description: Estudiantes de Ciencia de Datos e Inteligencia Artificial
summary:
What if the Gulf of Mexico is quietly losing the base of its food web?

We built a tool that turns 23 years of NASA satellite data into clear answers: what is changing in the ocean, where, how fast, and whether it’s real or just noise. It works for any region or variable.

Here’s what it revealed. The Gulf has warmed about 1 °C since 2003. Months that used to be extremely hot, 1 in 10, now happen 6 times out of 10. As the water warms, satellites show phytoplankton, the microscopic algae that feed the entire marine food web, declining in the deep Gulf and, most of all, on the Campeche Bank, by about 7% per decade. That’s one of Mexico’s most important fishing grounds.

Along the way, we found that two NASA satellites disagree, and learned to check our results against both.

Because you can’t protect what you don’t measure.
details:
What it does and how it works

Marine Ecosystem Change Explorer turns long records of NASA satellite data into four clear answers about the ocean: what is changing, where, by how much, and whether the change is statistically significant. We applied it to the Gulf of Mexico over 23 years (2003–2025, 276 months).

The workflow has five steps:

  1. Select. The tool searches NASA Earthdata (CMR) through earthaccess, removes duplicate files, downloads each monthly global file, clips it to the region of interest and deletes the rest. This cuts roughly 40 GB of global files to about 300 MB in minutes.
  2. Clean. Each month is masked to the official Gulf of Mexico ocean boundary (GCOOS). All variables are aligned on the same 4 km grid. The seasonal cycle is removed by computing monthly anomalies, and chlorophyll is analyzed on a log scale because its values are highly skewed.
  3. Measure. Sen’s slope gives the rate of change per decade with a 95% confidence interval, both for 7 marine regions and for about 2,300 map cells of 0.25°.
  4. Test. We use a Mann-Kendall test corrected for autocorrelation (Hamed-Rao), regression with robust errors, and false-discovery-rate control for multiple testing. We also correlate river-basin rainfall with coastal chlorophyll at time lags of 0–4 months, run a multiple regression with sea temperature, rainfall and El Niño, and estimate how the probability of extreme months has changed.
  5. Verify. Every trend is re-tested leaving out one year at a time, checked against chlorophyll fluorescence, and cross-validated with a second satellite (VIIRS). Each result is then graded as solid, weak or not detected.

The results feed an interactive web dashboard (nasa.cardenal-shekers.online). It has a 3D globe with monthly NASA layers and an analysis view where users pick a region, variable, period and season and get the trend, its significance, a trend map and the anomaly time series.

What we found

  • The Gulf warmed by 0.44–0.55 °C per decade in all regions, about +1 °C since 2003, and the warming is significant in 100% of the map cells.
  • Months that were extremely warm 1 time in 10 in 2003–2012 occurred 6 times in 10 in 2016–2025.
  • Chlorophyll-a, an indicator of the phytoplankton at the base of the food web, is declining on the Campeche Bank (about −7% per decade) and in the deep Gulf (about −3.5% per decade).
  • Warm months carry less chlorophyll in every region. On the Campeche Bank, warming statistically explains the whole decline.
  • Rain in river basins shows up in coastal chlorophyll 1–3 months later, except in the Yucatán Peninsula, where water flows underground.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Rigor. Simple tools often report trends that are just noise. With a classic test we would have flagged four chlorophyll trends; after all checks, two hold up.
  • Self-checking. A built-in negative control (Mississippi rain versus deep-Gulf chlorophyll) correctly comes out non-significant, showing the method does not invent relationships.
  • Early warning. The Campeche Bank is one of Mexico’s key fishing grounds, and the tool points to where monitoring is most urgent. A warmer Gulf also raises coral-bleaching risk and can fuel rapid hurricane intensification.
  • Education. For students and the public, the tool teaches how to be a data detective: an average can hide opposite changes, “not significant” does not mean “no change”, and a satellite sensor can age.

Tools and technologies

  • Data: NASA MODIS-Aqua chlorophyll-a, fluorescence and sea surface temperature (OB.DAAC, PO.DAAC); VIIRS-SNPP chlorophyll; GPM IMERG precipitation (GES DISC); NOAA ONI index; GCOOS Gulf boundary; USGS Watershed Boundary Dataset; Natural Earth.
  • Analysis: Python in Google Colab with earthaccess, xarray, netCDF4/h5netcdf, NumPy, pandas, GeoPandas, Shapely, regionmask, pymannkendall, statsmodels, SciPy and Matplotlib.
  • Web: HTML5, CSS and JavaScript, with Plotly and WebGL for the globe and charts, served from our own server with automated Earthdata ingestion.

What makes it creative

Most trend tools stop at “is the line going up?”. Ours questions its own answer. It corrects for the fact that consecutive months are not independent, controls false discoveries across thousands of map cells, tests a relationship that should not exist, and checks one satellite against another.

That last step changed our story. MODIS alone suggested “greener coasts” and a stable Gulf. Comparing it with VIIRS exposed a sensor drift: the coastal increase disappeared and a decline in the deep Gulf appeared.

Factors we considered

  • Seasonality: removed with monthly anomalies.
  • Skewed data: chlorophyll analyzed in log10.
  • Autocorrelation: 276 months behave like only 54–98 independent values.
  • Multiple testing: false-discovery-rate correction.
  • Optical limits: turbid river plumes can inflate satellite chlorophyll.
  • Chlorophyll is not productivity: it indicates phytoplankton biomass, not production rate.
  • Sensor aging: validated with VIIRS and with four different ways of joining the two satellite records.
  • Limited record length: chlorophyll trends need 30–60 years of continuous data to detect with confidence.
  • Correlation is not causation: results are presented as associations.
